title: Blog 1
content:
WINDOWS SERVER FLEET GUARD: MANAGING AND SECURING A LARGE WINDOWS INFRASTRUCTURE ON AWS Published on: AWS Study Group (Facebook)
A company that runs hundreds of Windows Server machines on-premises and on AWS often struggles to control access, keep configuration consistent and apply patches. Relying on RDP, bastion hosts or manual work on each machine takes time and increases security risk. This post summarizes how AWS automates the whole Windows Server lifecycle with AWS IAM Identity Center, EC2 Image Builder, AWS Systems Manager and Amazon CloudWatch.
Key points:
Three limits of manual administration: access that depends on RDP and bastion hosts widens the attack surface; manual configuration causes configuration drift; patching machine by machine makes it slow to fix vulnerabilities. Six main components: IAM Identity Center and IAM (identity, SSO), EC2 Image Builder (standard AMIs), State Manager (keeps configuration with PowerShell DSC), Fleet Manager (management and Remote Desktop in the browser), Patch Manager (scan and install patches), CloudWatch (metrics, Event Logs, alerts). Reusing Group Policy: existing GPOs can be converted to PowerShell DSC with ConvertFrom-GPO, also for servers that are not joined to a domain. Operating flow: Image Builder creates an AMI with the SSM Agent, the CloudWatch Agent and STIG security settings → State Manager applies the configuration by Tag → engineers sign in with IAM Identity Center and open Remote Desktop through Fleet Manager, with no need to open port 3389 → Patch Manager updates on a maintenance schedule → CloudWatch monitors. Access control: ABAC (permissions based on user and server attributes), AWS PrivateLink with VPC Endpoints (servers in a private subnet need no public Internet), Systems Manager Compliance (reports configuration and patch status). Limits to keep in mind: old applications that use Kerberos or NTLM may still need Active Directory; a Patch Baseline can delay urgent patches; CloudWatch Logs and VPC Endpoints cost more at large scale; a wrong configuration or patch can affect many machines at once, so group them into Dev, Staging and Production. Conclusion and thoughts:
The core of this approach is that each stage of the Windows Server lifecycle goes to its own service, all linked by Tags. Because engineers connect through Fleet Manager, port 3389 does not need to be open to the Internet, and the attack surface gets smaller. The approach still has limits: old applications that use Kerberos or NTLM may still need Active Directory, and because one wrong configuration or patch can affect many machines at once, servers should be grouped into Dev, Staging and Production and changes tested before they reach Production.
References:
AWS Blog: An AWS perspective on securely managing Windows Server infrastructure at scale. AWS Security Blog: Enable secure seamless single sign-on to Amazon EC2 Windows instances with AWS SSO. AWS Systems Manager User Guide: State Manager, Fleet Manager and Patch Manager. AWS Systems Manager, Amazon EC2 Image Builder, Amazon CloudWatch. Link: Post on AWS Study Group

title: Introduction
content:
Cost Guard A Windows EC2 instance is billed by the hour. A t3.small left running 24/7 costs about $31.04 per month, more than the $20 credit budget of this project. AWS Budgets can warn about cost, but its billing data refreshes only a few times per day, so it cannot stop a forgotten machine in time on its own. Cost Guard stops the machine automatically with three serverless layers. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will deploy Cost Guard with one CloudFormation template. The three layers work independently, and each one covers the weakness of the others.
Layer 1 – Schedule Guard: EventBridge Scheduler and a Lambda function stop the instance every day at 22:00 (Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh), whether or not anyone remembers. Layer 2 – Cost Meter: a Lambda function runs every 5 minutes, estimates the monthly cost from the running time and the hourly price, and stops the instance when the estimate reaches about $14. Layer 3 – Budget Backstop: an AWS Budget follows the real bill, and at 80% and 100% of $20 it triggers a Lambda function that stops the instance.

title: Blog 2
content:
MOVING MICROSOFT SYSTEMS TO AWS: 30% LOWER LICENSE COST AND 70% LOWER STORAGE COST Published on: AWS Study Group (Facebook)
Moving an old .NET Framework and SQL Server system to the cloud with a lift-and-shift approach, meaning it is moved as it is onto new infrastructure, does not solve the problems of license cost and scalability. This post retells a real example from TEKsystems Global Services (TGS): modernizing the whole Microsoft platform of a university into a cloud-native architecture on AWS. The result was 30% lower license cost and 70% lower storage cost.
Key points:
Analyze the system before changing it: the application was a monolith with 785,000 lines of code, 342 tables and 63 stored procedures. Before touching any code, the team ran three automated tools. CAST Highlight finds risks in the source code and barriers to moving to the cloud. CAST Imaging maps the data flow and the dependencies between components, which cut analysis time by 80%. Babelfish Compass checks how well SQL Server (T-SQL) can move to PostgreSQL. Analysis result: only about 20,000 of the 785,000 lines of code sit in the database layer, under 3% of the application. With the SQL Server dependency that small, replacing it was practical. From monolith to microservices: AWS Microservices Extractor for .NET analyzes the application and splits it into independent services instead of leaving everything in one block. From .NET Framework to .NET 8: Porting Assistant and AWS Transform for .NET help convert the source code. After the conversion, the application runs on Linux and AWS Graviton (Arm64). Database and storage: SQL Server is replaced by PostgreSQL, and Amazon FSx is replaced by Amazon S3. These two changes connect directly to the two cost savings. New architecture based on the AWS Well-Architected Framework: Amazon ECS runs Linux containers for compute. Amazon ELB and Route 53 handle load balancing and DNS. Amazon S3 and CloudFront deliver content. AWS WAF and Amazon Cognito handle security, and Amazon API Gateway manages the APIs. Amazon CloudWatch monitors the system. AWS Organizations provides central management and audit logs. Cost results: 30% lower commercial license cost and 70% lower storage cost. Conclusion and thoughts:
The 30% lower license cost and 70% lower storage cost came from analyzing the system first with tools such as CAST and Babelfish Compass, and then moving from .NET Framework to .NET 8 on Linux, from SQL Server to PostgreSQL and from Amazon FSx to Amazon S3. A lift-and-shift move alone would have left both costs where they were.
What I noticed most is the order of the work. The figure of 20,000 lines in the database layer only exists because of the analysis step, and that figure is what told the team that dropping SQL Server was feasible. Without it, the decision to change databases would have been hard to make. The post also shows that cloud modernization is more than moving servers to the cloud: restructuring the application, choosing suitable platforms and tuning the new architecture are what lower cost, improve scalability and make operations more efficient.
References:
AWS Blog: How TEKsystems modernized a university’s Microsoft workloads on AWS — aws.amazon.com/blogs/modernizing-with-aws AWS Transform for .NET (AWS Documentation, User Guide). AWS Microservices Extractor for .NET (AWS Documentation). Modernize Windows Workloads — aws.amazon.com/vi/transform/windows Link: Post on AWS Study Group

title: Prerequisites
content:
Prerequisites Prepare the items below before you start. The whole workshop runs in one region: US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1.
1. AWS account and permissions An AWS account with enough credit. The estimated cost of this workshop is about $8.05 (see section 5.7), so keep at least $20 of credit free. An IAM user to sign in. Do not use the root user. In a dedicated lab account, attaching the AdministratorAccess policy to this user is the simplest way. The user must be able to create CloudFormation stacks, IAM roles, EC2 instances, Lambda functions, DynamoDB tables, SNS topics, Parameter Store parameters, EventBridge Scheduler schedules, Budgets and CloudWatch alarms. MFA turned on for the root user and for the IAM user. 2. Network A default VPC in us-east-1. Open VPC → Your VPCs and check that one VPC is marked as default. If there is no default VPC, choose Actions → Create default VPC. Another option is to launch the lab instance yourself and pass its ID to the template (see 5.3). 3. Tools A web browser for the AWS Management Console. A mailbox that you can open, because Cost Guard sends its alerts by email and SNS needs you to confirm the address. Optional: AWS CLI v2, configured with aws configure, if you prefer the command line to the console. 4. Files The CloudFormation template cost-guard.yaml. It creates the whole system in one stack. 5. Know before you start The lab instance starts as soon as the stack is created. A Windows t3.small costs $0.0392 per hour in us-east-1, so test soon after the deployment and do not leave it running. On a Free Plan account only t3.micro, t3.small, t8i.micro and t8i.small can be launched. Plan about 45 minutes for the deployment and the three layer tests, not counting the wait for the daily schedule. Cost Guard never starts the instance by itself. You start it manually when you need it.

title: Proposal
content:
Cost Guard for Windows Labs on AWS A Serverless Three-Layer Credit Protection Solution 1. Executive Summary Cost Guard is designed for students and small teams who practice on AWS with a Free Plan account, to stop a Windows lab machine from using up the account credit. It protects one Windows EC2 instance (t3.small) and keeps the total project spend under a $20 budget. The system runs on AWS serverless services in US East (N. Virginia) and uses three protection layers: a scheduled stop with EventBridge Scheduler and Lambda, a near-real-time cost meter with Lambda, DynamoDB and Parameter Store, and a backstop with AWS Budgets and SNS. Alerts are sent by email, and all supporting services fit within the AWS Free Tier; the Windows EC2 instance is the only meaningful cost.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? AWS Free Plan credits are limited, and a Windows EC2 instance is billed by the hour for as long as it runs. A t3.small left running 24/7 costs about $31.04 per month, which is more than a $20 credit budget, and a machine forgotten after a lab session keeps spending credit. AWS Budgets can send cost alerts, but its billing data refreshes only a few times per day and it cannot stop the machine, so there is no real-time safeguard.
The Solution Cost Guard uses three complementary layers:
Layer 1 — Schedule Guard: An EventBridge Scheduler rule stops the instance outside lab hours. It does not depend on billing data, so it is the most reliable layer. The schedule only stops the machine; starting it stays a manual action so that no credit is spent while nobody is using it. Layer 2 — Cost Meter (original contribution): A Lambda function runs every 5 minutes. It estimates the cost of the running instance from its running time and a configured hourly price, and adds it to the estimated cost of earlier sessions in the current month. When the total crosses an internal threshold, the instance is stopped and an alert is sent through SNS. Layer 3 — Budget Backstop: AWS Budgets monitors the actual account spend. As spend approaches the limit, it triggers a Lambda function through SNS to stop the instance as the final safety net. Benefits and Return on Investment Under the planned usage of 120 lab hours per month, the estimated cost is about $7.12 per month. The same instance left running 24/7 would cost $31.04 per month. Cost Guard therefore avoids roughly $23.92 per month, about 77%, and keeps the project under the $20 budget. Layer 2 gives cost awareness within minutes of the machine starting, without waiting for billing data. The hourly price and the cost threshold are stored in Parameter Store instead of being hardcoded, so the system can be reused for other instance types or accounts.
Goals and Scope Cost Guard is built for students and small teams that run one Windows lab instance on an AWS account with limited credit.
Goals:
Stop the instance automatically when lab hours end. Stop the instance when the estimated monthly cost reaches the internal threshold (about $14). Stop the instance as a last resort when the actual spend reaches 80% and 100% of the $20 budget. Keep the total project spend under $20. Success criteria:
Layer 1: the instance is stopped at 22:00, and the Lambda log and the DynamoDB record show it. Layer 2: with simulated cost data, the instance is stopped within 5 minutes after the threshold is reached, and an alert email arrives. Layer 3: a test notification on the budget topic stops the instance and sends a confirmation email. Cost Explorer after cleanup shows a total spend under $20, and no instance or volume is left behind. Out of scope: managing more than one instance or account, starting the instance automatically, a web dashboard, and cost control for services other than the lab instance.
3. Solution Architecture The system runs in a single AWS Region (US East, N. Virginia) and uses only serverless or managed services. EventBridge drives the schedule and the periodic cost check. Lambda functions handle stop logic and cost estimation. DynamoDB records session activity. SNS delivers notifications. Parameter Store holds configuration. Each Lambda function has its own least-privilege IAM role.
AWS Services Used Amazon EC2 (Windows): The lab machine being protected (t3.small, Windows Server). A Free Plan account can only choose t3.micro, t3.small, t8i.micro and t8i.small; the team chose t3.small (2 vCPU, 2 GiB), the larger of the two t3 sizes, because 1 GiB is too little for Windows Server. Amazon EBS (gp3, 30 GB): The root volume of the lab machine. It is billed for the whole month, even while the instance is stopped. Amazon EventBridge: EventBridge Scheduler triggers the scheduled stop and runs the cost meter every 5 minutes. Both use schedules. AWS Lambda: Runs the logic of each protection layer. Amazon DynamoDB: Stores session activity and cost estimates. Amazon SNS: Sends email alerts when a threshold is crossed or an error occurs. AWS Budgets: Monitors actual spend and triggers the final protection layer. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: Stores the hourly price, the cost threshold and the budget limit. Amazon CloudWatch: Collects Lambda logs and raises alarms on function errors. AWS IAM: Provides a least-privilege execution role for each Lambda function. AWS CloudFormation: Packages the stack for repeatable deployment and clean teardown. AWS Cost Explorer: Compares the estimated cost with the actual cost at the end of the project. Component Design Scheduler Layer: EventBridge Scheduler → ScheduleHandler Lambda → stops the EC2 instance on a fixed schedule and writes the event to DynamoDB. Cost Meter: EventBridge Scheduler (every 5 minutes) → CostMeter Lambda → reads price and threshold from Parameter Store → calculates the estimated cost from session records in DynamoDB → if the threshold is exceeded, stops the instance and publishes an SNS alert. The threshold applies to the EC2 running cost only; the EBS volume is accounted for separately in the budget. Budget Backstop: AWS Budgets alarm → SNS topic → BudgetBackstop Lambda → stops the instance → sends a confirmation email. Notifications: One SNS topic for cost alerts to the user; one SNS topic for operational errors. Data: A DynamoDB table that logs instance start and stop events and the periodic cost estimate of each session. Security: Each Lambda function has its own IAM role, and its stop permission is limited to the target instance. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases
Research and design the architecture: Study the services used by the project and design the three protection layers (Month 1–2). Estimate the cost and check feasibility: Use the AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate the Windows instance and the supporting services, and check that the total stays under $20 (Month 2). Adjust the design to optimize cost and logic: Settle the Layer 2 cost rule, the threshold and the schedule, and keep the running hours to the plan of 120 hours per month (Month 2–3). Build, test and validate: Create the foundation (IAM roles, SNS topics, DynamoDB table, Parameter Store entries, AWS Budget), then deploy and test each layer: the scheduled stop, the threshold with simulated cost data, and the Budgets backstop with the CloudWatch alarms. Finish with an end-to-end validation and a comparison of the estimated and the actual cost in Cost Explorer (Month 3). Technical Requirements
AWS account and access: An AWS account with Free Plan credits, an IAM user (not the root user) and the US East (N. Virginia) Region. One email address receives the cost and error alerts. Protected resource: One Windows lab instance (t3.small) with a 30 GB gp3 root volume, planned for about 120 running hours per month. Three protection layers: A scheduled stop (EventBridge Scheduler and Lambda), a cost meter every 5 minutes (EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda, DynamoDB and Parameter Store) and a budget backstop (AWS Budgets, SNS and Lambda), each Lambda function with its own least-privilege IAM role. Monitoring and deployment: CloudWatch logs and alarms on function errors, SNS emails, and CloudFormation for repeatable deployment and clean teardown. Cost Explorer is used at the end to compare the estimated and the actual cost. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Month 1 (07/09 – 06/10/2026): Join the FCAJ program, read the internship rules and prepare the working environment. Then learn the AWS foundations: account setup, MFA, IAM, Budgets, Support, Console and CLI. Month 2 (07/10 – 06/11/2026): Study the services used by the project (Lambda, EventBridge, SNS, DynamoDB, Parameter Store, CloudWatch) and design the three layers. Month 3 (07/11 – 14/12/2026): Build, test and validate the solution. Week 1: Foundation and Layer 1, then test that the scheduled stop works at the set hour. Week 2: Layer 2, then test the threshold with simulated cost data and check that the instance stops within 5 minutes. Week 3: Layer 3 and the CloudWatch alarms, then test the budget notification and the error alarms. Week 4: End-to-end validation of the three layers, comparison of the estimated and the actual cost in Cost Explorer, and a check that no resource is left running after cleanup. Post-deployment: Keep the solution as a reusable template; extend it to other instance types or accounts by changing the Parameter Store values. 6. Budget Estimation The estimate was built with the AWS Pricing Calculator for US East (N. Virginia), using on-demand pricing and a planned usage of 120 lab hours per month (4 hours per day for 30 days).
AWS Pricing Calculator estimate: share link and PDF export.
Infrastructure Costs Amazon EC2 Windows (t3.small): 120 hours × $0.0392 per hour = $4.70 per month. In the Calculator the usage is entered directly as 120 Hours / Month, and the volume is priced in a separate EBS entry. Amazon EBS (gp3, 30 GB): $2.40 per month, billed for the whole month even when the instance is stopped. Public IPv4 address: $0.005 per hour for an in-use address, so 120 hours × $0.005 = $0.60 per month (not part of the Calculator estimate). AWS Lambda: about $0.02 per month (8,700 requests and 1,087.5 GB-seconds at 128 MB and 1 second per run), calculated without the Free Tier. Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand): about $0.002 per month (2,000 writes, 7,500 read request units and 0.001 GB of storage), left out of the Calculator because it is so small. Amazon CloudWatch: 3 standard alarms × $0.10 = $0.30 per month, plus about 0.01 GB of Lambda logs at $0.50 per GB ingested (about $0.005), calculated without the Free Tier. Parameter Store (standard parameters) and AWS Budgets (a tracking budget): $0.00 per month. EventBridge Scheduler is charged per invocation, and the first 14 million invocations per month are free. The project uses about 8,700 per month (the 5-minute schedule plus one daily stop), which is about $0.009 per month if the Free Tier is not counted. Amazon SNS (US East, standard topics): the first 1 million API requests and the first 1,000 email notifications per month are free. The project uses about 100 of each, so the cost is $0, and under $0.01 per month if the Free Tier is not counted. Delivery to Lambda has no per-message fee. Total: $7.12 per month for the services in the Calculator (EC2, EBS and Lambda), and about $8.05 when DynamoDB, the public IPv4 address, CloudWatch, EventBridge Scheduler and SNS are added, all calculated without the Free Tier. Both are under the $20 budget.
For comparison, the same instance running 24/7 (730 hours) costs $31.04 per month: $28.62 for EC2, $2.40 for EBS and about $0.02 for Lambda and DynamoDB.
The internal threshold of Layer 2 is set at about 70% of the budget ($14). At $0.0392 per hour this equals about 357 running hours, well above the planned 120 hours. The gap leaves room for the billing delay of Layer 3.
Cost Optimization Limit the running hours: the scheduled stop and the manual start keep the machine at about 120 hours per month instead of 730. Use services that charge per use and stay within the Free Tier: Lambda, DynamoDB on-demand, SNS and EventBridge. Use Parameter Store standard parameters, which have no charge. Use a 30 GB gp3 volume (the default size of the Windows image) with no extra IOPS or throughput. Compare instance types in the Pricing Calculator before launch and keep the smallest type that runs the lab comfortably. Avoid an Elastic IP, which is billed while allocated. Delete every resource after the demo and confirm it in Cost Explorer. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Running out of credit midway because a machine is left running or a layer fails: high impact, medium probability. Three people sharing one AWS account, so one person can overwrite the settings of another or stop a machine that a teammate is using (for example, lowering the threshold for a test): medium impact, medium probability. A schedule set with the wrong time zone, so the stop runs at the wrong hour. The cron expression of an EventBridge rule is read in UTC, so it is easy to be several hours off: medium impact, medium probability. A schedule that never triggers the Lambda function, because the cron expression is written wrongly or the function has no permission for EventBridge to invoke it: medium impact, medium probability. Budgets data arriving late or being misread, because billing data refreshes only a few times per day: high impact, high probability (by design). Layer 2 estimate diverging from the actual bill: medium impact, medium probability. A Lambda function stopping the wrong instance because of a misconfigured IAM role: high impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Credit running out: Layer 1 stops the instance every day at a fixed hour, and Layer 2 and Layer 3 stop it when the cost rises. One failing layer does not remove the other two. Shared account: each person uses their own IAM user, only one person launches the instance, and any change to the threshold, the price or the schedule is announced to the team and put back after the test. Time zone: use EventBridge Scheduler for the daily stop, because it lets the time zone be set explicitly (Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh) instead of relying on UTC. Test it once with a stop time a few minutes ahead before relying on it. Schedule not triggering: check the cron expression in the schedule preview, and confirm that the Lambda function allows EventBridge to invoke it (its resource-based policy). Look at the invocation count and the log after the first test. Budgets delay: treat Layer 3 only as the last safety net, and rely on Layer 2 for fast reaction. Estimate drift: set the threshold below the budget and compare the estimate with Cost Explorer at the end of the project. Wrong instance: each Lambda role can stop only the target instance. Contingency Plans If a Lambda layer fails, stop the instance manually from the AWS Console and disable the EventBridge schedules. If the credit runs out during the project, terminate the Windows instance immediately. If the $20 budget is not enough, reduce the daily lab hours or switch to a smaller instance type and update the estimate. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements Reaction time: From the moment the estimated cost reaches the threshold to the moment the instance is stopped is under 5 minutes, which is one Cost Meter interval. Correct stops: In the tests, each layer stops the instance every time it should, and never stops it when the cost is below the threshold. The workshop records the number of test runs and their results. Spend: The total project spend stays under $20, confirmed by Cost Explorer after cleanup. Observability: All three layers can be followed through Lambda logs, SNS emails and the DynamoDB session record. Long-term Value Because the instance ID, hourly price and threshold are stored in Parameter Store, the same system can protect another Windows lab account by changing those values, without changing code.

title: Blog 3
content:
COST GUARD: THREE SERVERLESS LAYERS THAT STOP A WINDOWS INSTANCE TO PROTECT AWS FREE PLAN CREDIT Published on: AWS Study Group (Facebook)
My team (AwsAILearner67, FCAJ) runs labs in one shared AWS Free Plan account with limited credit. The most common problem is not technical but human: people finish studying and forget to stop the instance. A Windows t3.small running 24/7 costs about $31.04 a month (EC2 $28.62 + EBS $2.40), more than the whole project’s $20 budget.
AWS Budgets can send alert emails, but it has two limits: billing data only updates a few times a day, and Budgets does not stop instances. So we built Cost Guard: three independent layers watching one instance, so if one layer fails the other two are still there.
The three layers:
Layer 1 – Scheduled stop: EventBridge Scheduler calls the Lambda CostGuard-ScheduleHandler at 22:00 every day in the Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh time zone. If the instance is running, the function calls StopInstances; if it is already stopped, it only records schedule_noop. This layer needs no billing data, so it is the most reliable. We deliberately do not start the instance automatically: whoever needs it starts it, so nothing is billed while nobody is using it. Layer 2 – Cost meter (the part we built ourselves): every 5 minutes, the Lambda CostGuard-CostMeter checks the instance. If it is running, the function adds the cost of those 5 minutes ($0.0392/hour × 5/60 ≈ $0.0033) to the month’s total and stores a record in DynamoDB. When the total reaches the $14 threshold, it stops the instance and sends an email through SNS. It does not wait for billing, so it reacts within minutes. Layer 3 – Last safety net: an AWS Budget of $20 alerts at 80% and 100% of actual spend. Budgets publishes to the SNS topic costguard-budgets, which calls the Lambda CostGuard-BudgetBackstop to stop the instance and send a confirmation email. Billing is slow, so this layer is the last resort. On top of that, a CloudWatch alarm watches the errors of all three Lambda functions and emails through a separate topic, costguard-errors. If a layer breaks, the team knows right away instead of finding out when the credit is gone.
Why the threshold is $14: Layer 2’s threshold is about 70% of the budget. At $0.0392/hour, $14 is about 357 running hours, far more than the planned 120 lab hours a month. The remaining $6 covers the billing delay of Layer 3. The price, the threshold and the instance ID live in Parameter Store instead of being hard-coded, so using it for another instance only means changing the values.
Real test results (us-east-1, 22 and 25/11/2026):
Layer Test Result 1 Invoke the function directly while the instance is running Instance stopped after 3 seconds 2 Lower the threshold to 0.001 and wait for the next run CostMeter stopped the instance 3 min 47 s after the threshold was saved (from CloudTrail) 3 Publish a test message to the costguard-budgets topic Instance stopped after 7 seconds All three runs left a record in DynamoDB (schedule_stop, auto_stop, budget_stop) and an email in the team inbox. Remember to set the threshold back to 14 after testing.
Cost: according to the AWS Pricing Calculator, for 120 lab hours a month: EC2 $4.70 + EBS $2.40 + Lambda $0.02 = $7.12/month. With the public IPv4 address, CloudWatch and other services it is about $8.05. Compared with $31.04 for an instance left running, Cost Guard saves about $23.92 a month (~77%). The “protection” part (Lambda, on-demand DynamoDB, SNS, Scheduler, Parameter Store) costs almost nothing.
Conclusion and thoughts:
Cost protection should have several layers: one based on time, one on an estimate, one on the real bill. Each covers the weakness of the others. Each Lambda function has its own IAM role, and StopInstances is allowed only on the lab instance. A misconfiguration cannot stop someone else’s instance. The lab instance opens no inbound port and requires IMDSv2. Everything lives in one CloudFormation template, so deleting the stack removes almost everything. In our real cleanup we still had to delete two things created outside the stack by hand: the IAM role that the Scheduler console created, and the cf-templates bucket holding the uploaded template. AWS CLI
aws cloudformation deploy \ --region us-east-1 \ --stack-name CostGuard \ --template-file cost-guard.yaml \ --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \ --parameter-overrides AlertEmail=you@example.com Step 2 – Confirm the email subscriptions Open the mailbox. title: Layer 1 – Schedule Guard
content:
Layer 1 – Schedule Guard Layer 1 stops the lab instance at a fixed time every day. It does not read any cost or billing data, so it is the most reliable of the three layers.
How it works EventBridge Scheduler invokes the Lambda function CostGuard-ScheduleHandler every day at 22:00 (time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh), with the event {"action": "stop"}. The function reads the instance ID from /costguard/instance-id. It calls DescribeInstances. If the instance is running, it calls StopInstances. In any other state, it does nothing, so a repeated call is safe. It writes a record to CostGuardSessions (schedule_stop or schedule_noop). If anything fails, it publishes the error to costguard-errors and raises the error, so the CloudWatch alarm in 5.6 can see it. The schedule only stops the machine. Starting it stays a manual action, so no credit is spent while nobody uses the lab.
Why EventBridge Scheduler An EventBridge rule reads a cron expression in UTC, so a stop planned for 22:00 in Vietnam must be written as 15:00. EventBridge Scheduler accepts a time zone, so the expression below says exactly what it means. Scheduler also invokes the function through its own role, so the function needs no extra resource-based permission.
StopSchedule: Type: AWS::Scheduler::Schedule Properties: Name: costguard-daily-stop ScheduleExpression: !Ref StopCron # default cron(0 22 * * ? *) ScheduleExpressionTimezone: !Ref StopScheduleTimezone # default Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh FlexibleTimeWindow: Mode: "OFF" Target: Arn: !GetAtt ScheduleHandlerFunction.Arn RoleArn: !GetAtt SchedulerRole.Arn Input: '{"action": "stop"}' Step 1 – Look at the schedule Open EventBridge → Scheduler → Schedules and choose costguard-daily-stop. Check the cron expression, the time zone and the target CostGuard-ScheduleHandler. Check: costguard-daily-stop and costguard-cost-meter are both Enabled. Open costguard-daily-stop to see the expression cron(0 22 * * ? *), the time zone Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh and the target CostGuard-ScheduleHandler.
Step 2 – Test the function Make sure the instance is running (EC2 console). Open Lambda → CostGuard-ScheduleHandler → Test. Create a test event with the body {} and choose Test. Open the EC2 console and refresh. Open DynamoDB → Tables → CostGuardSessions → Explore table items. Result: the function returns schedule_stop with state_before set to running. The instance goes from stopping to stopped. The table has a new item with event = schedule_stop.
Check: the test status is Succeeded and the result contains schedule_stop with state_before set to running.
Run the test a second time while the instance is stopped. Result: the function returns schedule_noop and the instance is not touched.
Check: this time the result is schedule_noop with state_before set to stopped, so the function did not call StopInstances again.
Step 3 – Test the real schedule (optional) Start the instance again. Open CloudFormation → CostGuard → Update, keep the current template and change StopCron to a time a few minutes ahead, for example cron(25 15 * * ? *) at 15:25 Vietnam time. Wait until that time and check the instance state. Update the stack again and put cron(0 22 * * ? *) back. Result: the instance is stopped at the chosen time in Vietnam time, not seven hours earlier or later.
In our own run we did not change StopCron; we checked the real 22:00 run on 22/11/2026 instead. The schedule invoked the function at 15:00:02 UTC (22:00 Vietnam time). The instance was already stopped, so the function only wrote schedule_noop.
Check: the log shows an invocation at 15:00 UTC (22:00 Vietnam time) and a schedule_noop line with the instance ID.
Check: there is a new item with event = schedule_noop and a timestamp that matches the schedule run.
In this section, you looked at the schedule costguard-daily-stop, which runs at 22:00 Vietnam time through EventBridge Scheduler, and tested the CostGuard-ScheduleHandler function. When the instance was running, the function stopped it and wrote schedule_stop; when it was already stopped, the function only wrote schedule_noop. title: Layer 2 – Cost Meter
content:
Layer 2 – Cost Meter Layer 2 estimates how much the lab instance has cost this month and stops it when the estimate reaches a threshold. It reacts within minutes, because it uses the running time of the instance and a configured hourly price, not billing data. This layer is the original contribution of the project.
How it works EventBridge Scheduler invokes CostGuard-CostMeter every 5 minutes (rate(5 minutes)).
The function reads the instance ID, the hourly price and the threshold from Parameter Store.
If the instance is not running, the function stops here.
If it is running, the function calculates the cost of this interval:
interval cost = price per hour × 5 ÷ 60 With $0.0392 per hour, each run adds about $0.0033.
It reads all sample items of the current calendar month (UTC) from CostGuardSessions and adds them up. This is the monthly total.
It writes a new sample item with the interval cost and the new monthly total.
If the total reaches the threshold, it stops the instance, writes an auto_stop item and publishes an alert to costguard-alerts.
What the threshold covers. The estimate counts the running cost of the EC2 instance only. The EBS volume ($2.40 per month) is a fixed cost and is counted separately in the budget.
After an automatic stop. The monthly total stays above the threshold, so if you start the instance again, the next run stops it again within 5 minutes. The machine stays locked until the next calendar month. This keeps the credit safe, and the price is that the lab cannot be used for the rest of that month.
Known limits. A session shorter than one interval may not be counted, and the month changes at midnight UTC, which is 07:00 in Vietnam.
Step 1 – Look at the configuration Open Systems Manager → Parameter Store and read /costguard/price-per-hour (0.0392) and /costguard/cost-threshold (14). Open EventBridge → Scheduler → Schedules and check that costguard-cost-meter is enabled and uses rate(5 minutes). Check: all four parameters exist (budget-limit, cost-threshold, instance-id and price-per-hour) in the Standard tier, which has no charge.
Check: the value is 0.0392. Open /costguard/cost-threshold the same way; its value must be 14.
Check: costguard-cost-meter is Enabled. Open it to see the expression rate(5 minutes) and the target CostGuard-CostMeter.
Step 2 – Test the threshold You do not wait for the real threshold of $14. You lower it so that the next run crosses it.
Start the instance and wait until it is running. Open Parameter Store → /costguard/cost-threshold → Edit and change the value to 0.001. Write down the clock time when you save. Wait for the next run, at most 5 minutes. Check the EC2 console, your mailbox and the DynamoDB table. Put the threshold back to 14. Do not update the CloudFormation stack during the test, because that would also reset the value. Result: the instance goes to stopping and then stopped. You receive the email “CostGuard: instance stopped (cost threshold)”. The table has a sample item and an auto_stop item.
Check: the value is now 0.001. Write down the time you saved it for Step 3.

You deploy the whole system with one CloudFormation template, test each layer on purpose, review security and cost, and delete everything at the end so that no charge is left behind.

AWS Budgets: the monthly budget and its 80% and 100% alerts. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: price, threshold and budget limit. Amazon CloudWatch: logs and alarms on function errors. AWS IAM: one least-privilege role for each function. AWS CloudFormation: the whole system in one stack. AWS Cost Explorer: the comparison of real cost and estimate after cleanup. title: Layer 3 – Budget Backstop and Monitoring
content:
Layer 3 – Budget Backstop and Monitoring Layer 3 is the last safety net. It follows the actual spend of the account, so it is slow by design: billing data refreshes only a few times per day. This step also covers the CloudWatch alarms that tell you when one of the three functions fails.
How it works AWS Budgets tracks the monthly cost of the account against a limit of $20 (CostGuard-Budget). When the actual cost goes above 80% and above 100% of the limit, Budgets sends a notification to the SNS topic costguard-budgets and an email to you. The topic invokes the Lambda function CostGuard-BudgetBackstop. The function stops the instance if it is running, writes budget_stop (or budget_noop) to CostGuardSessions and publishes a confirmation to costguard-alerts. How the layers work together Layer 1 stops the machine at a fixed hour. Layer 2 stops it within minutes when the estimated cost reaches the threshold. Layer 3 stops it when the real bill gets close to the limit. Any layer can stop the machine, no layer can start it, and stopping a stopped machine does nothing. So the layers do not conflict, and one layer failing does not remove the other two.
Step 1 – Look at the budget Open Billing and Cost Management → Budgets and choose CostGuard-Budget. Check the monthly limit and the two alerts (80% and 100%, actual cost). Check: Budget amount is $20.00, Period is Monthly and Health status is Healthy.
Check: there are exactly two alerts on actual cost, at 80% ($16.00) and 100% ($20.00). Email verification must show the address as verified; if it is still Pending, choose Resend verification and confirm it in your mailbox, otherwise Budgets sends no email.
Step 2 – Test the Budget Backstop You do not wait for the real bill to grow. You send a message to the topic yourself.
Start the instance and wait until it is running. Open SNS → Topics → costguard-budgets → Publish message. Use any subject and message, and choose Publish message. Check the EC2 console, your mailbox and the DynamoDB table. Result: the instance goes to stopping and then stopped. You receive the email “CostGuard: budget notification handled”. The table has an item with event = budget_stop.
Check: the console reports that the message was published and shows a Message ID.
Check: there is one invocation (START, END and REPORT lines) right after the publish time and no ERROR line.
Check: there is a new item with event = budget_stop.
Check: the email subject is “CostGuard: budget notification handled”.
Step 3 – Look at the alarms Open CloudWatch → Alarms. You see three alarms: CostGuard-ScheduleHandler-Errors, CostGuard-CostMeter-Errors and CostGuard-BudgetBackstop-Errors. Each one watches the Errors metric of its function and sends a message to costguard-errors when the metric is above 0. Open CloudWatch → Log groups. The three /aws/lambda/CostGuard-* log groups keep their logs for 14 days. Check: all three alarms exist, State is OK, Actions shows Actions enabled and the condition is Errors > 0.
Check: the Retention column shows 2 weeks (14 days) for all three log groups.
Step 4 – Test an error scenario This test makes CostGuard-CostMeter fail on purpose to check that the alarm and the email work.
Open Parameter Store → /costguard/instance-id → Edit. Write down the real instance ID first, then replace the value with i-00000000000000000. Wait up to 10 minutes. The function runs every 5 minutes and the alarm uses a 5-minute period. Check the log of CostGuard-CostMeter, the alarm state and your mailbox. Put the real instance ID back. Result: the function fails, you receive an email from costguard-errors, and the alarm CostGuard-CostMeter-Errors changes to In alarm. After you restore the ID and the next run succeeds, the alarm returns to OK.
Check: State is In alarm after the failed run of the function.
Check: State is back to OK after the next successful run.
Check: the email subject starts with ALARM: and names the alarm that fired.
In this section, you looked at the AWS Budget CostGuard-Budget ($20, alerts at 80% and 100%), tested CostGuard-BudgetBackstop by publishing a message to the costguard-budgets topic, and checked the three error alarms by making CostGuard-CostMeter fail on purpose. All three layers have now been tested, and you are told when one of them breaks.

title: Security and Cost Review
content:
Security and Cost Review This step reviews how Cost Guard handles security, what it costs and how to keep the cost low.
1. Security One IAM role for each function. The three Lambda functions have separate roles, so a mistake in one function cannot use the permissions of another. The permission to stop an instance is limited to the ARN of the protected instance:
{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "ec2:StopInstances", "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:<account-id>:instance/<instance-id>" } ec2:DescribeInstances is allowed on all resources, because this action does not support resource-level restriction. The other permissions are limited to the parameters, the table and the topics that the function uses.
No credentials in code. The functions use their execution roles. The Parameter Store values are only the hourly price, the threshold, the budget limit and the instance ID.
Services call each other with their own roles. EventBridge Scheduler uses a role that can invoke only the two functions. The topic policy of costguard-budgets lets only the Budgets service in your own account publish.
No open ports. The lab instance in this workshop uses its own security group, costguard-lab-no-inbound, which has no inbound rule at all, and it requires IMDSv2. If you let the template create the instance instead, it uses the default security group of the default VPC, which only allows traffic from members of the same group.
Check: open EC2 → Security Groups → costguard-lab-no-inbound. Inbound rules count is 0 Permission entries and the Inbound rules tab says “No security group rules found”.
To check: open IAM → Roles, choose each CostGuard role and read its policy. The only action that touches EC2 state is StopInstances on one instance.
Check: ec2:StopInstances has the ARN of exactly one instance as its Resource, ec2:DescribeInstances is *, and ssm:GetParameter is limited to /costguard/instance-id. Read the other two roles the same way.
2. Cost estimation The estimate was made with the AWS Pricing Calculator for US East (N. Virginia), using on-demand prices and 120 lab hours per month. Prices are without the Free Tier.
Amazon EC2 Windows (t3.small): 120 hours × $0.0392 = $4.70 Amazon EBS (gp3, 30 GB): $2.40, billed for the whole month even while the instance is stopped Public IPv4 address: 120 hours × $0.005 = $0.60 AWS Lambda: about $0.02 Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand): about $0.002 Amazon CloudWatch (3 alarms and logs): about $0.31 EventBridge Scheduler and Amazon SNS: under $0.01 each The services in the Calculator (EC2, EBS and Lambda) add up to $7.12 per month (estimate). With the other services added, the total is about $8.05 per month, under the $20 budget. The same instance running 24/7 would cost about $31.04 per month, so Cost Guard avoids about $23.92 per month.
Check: Monthly cost is 7.12 USD, made of Amazon EC2 4.70 USD, Amazon EBS 2.40 USD and AWS Lambda 0.02 USD, in US East (N. Virginia).
3. Cost optimization Limit the running hours. The scheduled stop and the manual start keep the machine near 120 hours instead of 730. Use pay-per-use services in their free allowance: Lambda, DynamoDB on-demand, SNS and EventBridge Scheduler. Use standard parameters in Parameter Store, which have no charge. Keep the 30 GB gp3 volume and add no extra IOPS or throughput. Do not attach an Elastic IP, which is billed while it is allocated. Delete all resources after the workshop (see 5.8). In this section, you reviewed the security of Cost Guard (one IAM role per function, StopInstances allowed on one instance only, no inbound ports), the estimated cost of about $7.12 a month for 120 lab hours compared with $31.04 for running 24/7, and the ways to keep the cost low.

title: Clean Up
content:
Clean Up You have now completed the whole Cost Guard workshop: the lab machine is protected by three layers, and all three have been tested. Only the final step is left, which is to clean up and delete everything you created so that nothing is billed afterwards. The screenshots below come from our own clean-up on 26/11/2026 in us-east-1, done with an IAM user, not the root user.
Order matters: delete the CostGuard stack first, then the lab instance, then the few resources that were created outside the stacks.
Step 1 – Look at what you have Open CloudFormation → Stacks. In our account there were two stacks: CostGuard (the three protection layers) and costguard-instance (the Windows lab machine, passed to CostGuard as ExistingInstanceId). Open the Resources tab of each stack to see what it will delete. CostGuard holds 29 resources: Lambda functions, roles, log groups, schedules, the DynamoDB table, the SNS topics, the Budget and the alarms. Note the instance ID in EC2 → Instances, so you can check later that it is terminated. Step 2 – Delete the CostGuard stack Select CostGuard and choose Delete. Type the stack name to confirm. The stack goes to DELETE_IN_PROGRESS. The Events tab shows each resource being deleted. Wait for DELETE_COMPLETE. The stack disappears from the active list; to see it again, set the filter to Deleted. With the CLI:
aws cloudformation delete-stack --region us-east-1 --stack-name CostGuard aws cloudformation wait stack-delete-complete --region us-east-1 --stack-name CostGuard Step 3 – Delete the lab instance If CostGuard created the instance itself (empty ExistingInstanceId), Step 2 already terminated it; skip to Step 4.
If you passed ExistingInstanceId, the stack did not create that instance and does not delete it. We created it with a separate stack, so we deleted that stack:
Select costguard-instance, choose Delete and type the name. The instance becomes Terminated. AWS hides terminated instances after about an hour; they cost nothing. The active stack list is now empty, and the Deleted filter shows both stacks. If you made the instance by hand, terminate it in EC2 → Instances → Instance state → Terminate instance.
Step 4 – Delete what the stacks did not create Two things were created outside the stacks during the project. Check for them even if you followed the guide exactly.
IAM role made by the Scheduler console. When you create a schedule in the EventBridge Scheduler console and choose Create new role, AWS creates a role Amazon_EventBridge_Scheduler_LAMBDA_* and a policy Amazon-EventBridge-Scheduler-Execution-Policy-*. Deleting the stack does not remove them.
Open IAM → Roles, search Amazon_EventBridge_Scheduler. Open the role and check that its policy only invokes a CostGuard-* function. Delete the role, then delete the policy in IAM → Policies (it has no attachment left). S3 bucket cf-templates-*. When you upload a template file in the CloudFormation console, AWS stores it in a bucket named cf-templates-<random>-us-east-1. Delete it only if it holds nothing but this workshop’s templates.
Open the bucket and check its objects. Ours held only costguard and cost-guard templates. Choose Empty, type permanently delete, and confirm. Choose Delete, type the bucket name, and confirm. Step 5 – Check that nothing is left Check each console in us-east-1:
EC2 → Instances: no lab instance is running or stopped (a Terminated line is fine). EC2 → Volumes: no volume is left behind. EC2 → Elastic IPs: none allocated. EC2 → Security Groups and Launch Templates: only default is left, no lab launch template. Lambda: no CostGuard-* function. DynamoDB: no CostGuardSessions table. EventBridge → Scheduler and Rules: no costguard-* schedule and no CostGuard rule. SNS: no costguard-* topic and no subscription to it. CloudWatch: no CostGuard-* alarm and no /aws/lambda/CostGuard-* log group. Budgets: no CostGuard-Budget. Budgets made by other people in a shared account can stay. Systems Manager → Parameter Store: no /costguard/ parameter. IAM → Roles: no CostGuard-* role. S3: no cf-templates-* bucket of this workshop. The same check in CloudShell.
